edition.deck: Nvidia’s chief is back after a dramatic reversal, while fresh reporting examines Russia’s war losses and Ukraine’s strikes far from the front.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise overnight developments and genuinely new reporting. The repeated COP31 outcome is not carried forward; the selected Ukraine story reflects a new claim of responsibility for the Benghazi attack.

content.headline: Trump-backed Nvidia U-turn puts export controls and board independence under
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s Nvidia intervention raises export-control questions
content.standfirst: Jensen Huang has returned as Nvidia chief after Donald Trump said he persuaded the board to reverse its decision. The comeback has revived questions about chip exports to China and the independence of corporate oversight.

image.caption: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, at an AI event in San Jose.

sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after affair with alleged spy as Trump says 'I made the deal'
Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
US adds Megaspeed, AI firm at center of Nvidia scandal, to trade blacklist
Republican senators criticize Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang

segments.body: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is suspected by US officials of links to Chinese intelligence. Alice Huang and China deny the allegations. Donald Trump said he had convinced Nvidia’s board to bring the chief executive back.

segments.title: A market-moving reversal
segments.body: Nvidia shares rose about 32% on Monday, adding more than $1tn to the company’s market value, while the news helped lift US markets. The share price had fallen after Huang’s departure. Nvidia’s board says it received input from senior US government officials and considers his return no national security risk.

segments.title: Questions remain for Congress
segments.body: The US has placed Megaspeed and subsidiaries on a trade blacklist as it investigates suspected breaches of export controls. Lawmakers from both parties are seeking answers about the government’s role in Huang’s return and whether Nvidia chips reached China. Huang is due before House committees on 1 December; a Senate banking committee hearing is scheduled for 3 December.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s review of Trump’s financial disclosures found repeated Nvidia share purchases and sales since he returned to office. Trump and the White House deny that he has profited from the presidency; the disclosures do not establish why he intervened.

content.headline: Leaked Russian records point to more than 460,000 war-related deaths
content.shortHeadline: Leaked records show more than 460,000 Russian war deaths
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s analysis of a large cache of Russian death certificates offers a rare view of the human cost of the invasion. The records are incomplete, and the Kremlin has not published an updated official toll since 2022.

sources.originalTitle: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war

segments.body: The Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths linked to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine between February 2022 and September 2026, using records from a cache of more than 11 million death certificates. The analysis says war became the leading recorded cause of death among Russian men under 65 in 2025.

segments.title: A costly advance
segments.body: The analysis records close to 200,000 deaths in 2025, the deadliest year in the dataset. Russia’s frontline gains since the start of 2023 amounted to about 8,000 square kilometres, according to the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState. A Russia expert cited by the Guardian says the data points to a manpower problem, but the figures do not establish the full battlefield toll.

segments.title: Suicides may be undercounted
segments.body: A separate analysis of the records found 1,087 military deaths classified as suicides since the invasion began, and another 885 firearm deaths of “undetermined intent” in or near Ukraine. Experts say the latter category may conceal suicides; activists working with deserters believe the total is higher. Some deaths may instead be recorded as combat losses.

content.headline: Ukraine confirms Benghazi strikes as attacks on Russian ships reach farther
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian ships off Libya
content.standfirst: President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukrainian forces attacked Russian vessels in Libya, including a corvette he says was sunk. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for a separate strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland.

image.caption: A Ukrainian sea drone approaches a vessel off Benghazi in footage shared by Volodymyr Zelensky.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine rammer russiske skibe langt fra frontlinjen: 'Rusland har ikke helle nogen steder længere'
Angreb på russiske skibe varsler ny fase af krigen, siger eksperter
What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war

segments.body: Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine was behind attacks on the Russian corvette Merkury and cargo ship MV Angara in Benghazi, Libya. He said the corvette was sunk and a Russian military helicopter destroyed. Ukraine says the ships were linked to the transport or protection of military supplies; those claims are attributed to Kyiv.

segments.title: A wider reach—and a risk
segments.body: The attacks follow a separate strike on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Ukraine has not claimed that attack, although Finnish military officials and analysts cited by DR consider Ukrainian involvement likely. Analysts say the incidents show Ukraine can target Russian vessels far from its own territory, but warn that activity near allies could strain Kyiv’s relationships with them.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s Frank Gardner sees the Benghazi attack as another sign that the war is spreading beyond Ukraine. He warns that a strike on Russian ships in a harbour in a country not party to the war could set a dangerous precedent for shipping.

content.headline: Nato chief responds to reports of possible Russian nuclear satellite
content.shortHeadline: Nato vows to defend against space threats after Russia reports
content.standfirst: German media, citing anonymous military and intelligence sources, report that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Nato says it will defend against threats in space; Moscow rejects the allegations, which have not been independently confirmed.

image.caption: Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans for nuclear weapons in space.

sources.originalTitle: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports

segments.body: Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would defend against threats in space after German media reported intelligence warnings of a possible Russian satellite launch in the coming weeks. The reports, based on anonymous German military and intelligence sources, describe a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead that could disrupt or destroy other satellites.

segments.title: Reports disputed
segments.body: The reports’ originating country is unclear. The Kremlin said it had not seen the latest claims and dismissed reports based on unnamed sources; Russia’s embassy in Berlin called them unfounded. German officials did not confirm the allegations, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they showed the level of escalation Russia was prepared to pursue.

segments.title: A treaty and a wider arms race
segments.body: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit. The BBC notes that other countries are also pursuing military capabilities in space, including systems that could target satellites. The reports do not establish that Russia has decided to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

content.headline: Iranian singer and four others flogged after performance without hijab, lawyers
content.shortHeadline: Iranian singer flogged after performing without hijab, lawyers say
content.standfirst: Parastoo Ahmadi and four male members of her band and production team were given 74 lashes in Qom, a defence lawyer told the BBC. They had been convicted over a concert livestreamed in 2024.

image.caption: Parastoo Ahmadi performs in a concert livestreamed in December 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

segments.body: Parastoo Ahmadi and four male members of her band and production team were flogged in the Iranian city of Qom, a lawyer on their defence team told the BBC. Each was given 74 lashes, the lawyer said. Ahmadi had performed in a sleeveless dress at a concert livestreamed in December 2024.

segments.title: Appeal failed
segments.body: A court convicted Ahmadi and eight others in June of “offending public decency” through the publication of material it called obscene and indecent. The defendants denied the accusation. An appeals court rejected their challenge in September and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said. The sentence also included a two-year ban on audiovisual activities and leaving Iran.

content.headline: South African communities take precautions amid violence against women
content.shortHeadline: South African communities organise as violence against women persists
content.standfirst: The BBC reports that 581 women were killed in South Africa between July and September, in the first police figures broken down by gender. Families and communities describe seeking answers and organising their own safety measures.

sources.originalTitle: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

segments.body: South African police recorded 581 women killed between July and September, alongside 5,590 murders overall. It is the first time the police have published murder figures broken down by gender, so the data cannot show whether killings of women have risen or fallen compared with previous years.

segments.title: Seeking answers and safety
segments.body: Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi says he learned of his daughter Okuhle’s death through a Facebook post. Months later, he said no one had been arrested and that he was seeking CCTV footage and other leads himself. The BBC says the police had not responded to its request for comment by publication.

segments.title: Community responses
segments.body: In Kokstad, residents have organised night patrols and a voluntary curfew for women and children after several bodies were found in the area. Women in Johannesburg have also adapted their running routines, including by running in groups and carrying whistles or pepper spray. These precautions coexist with calls for stronger official action.

content.headline: Iowa explosives blast awaits governor after court partly clears way
content.shortHeadline: Iowa explosives blast awaits governor’s agreement after court ruling
content.standfirst: Donald Trump ordered the Army to hold off on detonating degraded explosives until a federal court and Iowa’s incoming governor agreed. An appeals court has partly cleared the way, but the governor-elect has not said whether he consents.

image.caption: Residents in Iowa have raised concerns about plans to destroy degraded explosives.

sources.originalTitle: Trump orders US military not to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa for now

segments.body: The US Army plans to detonate 68 drums containing lead azide, a volatile compound at an Iowa ammunition plant. President Donald Trump ordered the military not to proceed unless the Eighth Circuit appeals court and governor-elect Rob Sand agreed. Sand, who takes office in January, has not said whether he supports the operation.

segments.title: Safety and environmental concerns
segments.body: The Army says the material has degraded and could explode spontaneously, with the risk increasing as temperatures fall. The appeals court said the emergency permit included safeguards intended to limit dust dispersal. Environmental groups that sued to stop the detonation say the Army has not provided enough public information or protection.

segments.title: Timing remains uncertain
segments.body: The Army said it intended to carry out the detonation on Wednesday, but it was unclear whether Trump’s order or the court’s decision would change that plan. The EPA says no level of lead exposure is considered safe; the agency granted an emergency permit, arguing that an uncontrolled explosion could pose a greater threat.

content.headline: UK sanctions Myanmar military figures after ICJ genocide ruling
content.shortHeadline: UK sanctions Myanmar military figures after genocide ruling
content.standfirst: Britain has sanctioned five senior military figures after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The case concerned the 2017 military campaign, which drove hundreds of thousands from their homes.

image.caption: Rohingya people fled to Bangladesh during the violence in Myanmar in 2017.

sources.originalTitle: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
14 lande anerkender dom om folkedrab i Myanmar

segments.body: The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military figures after the International Court of Justice ruled that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. The court found by a majority that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from the evidence it considered. Myanmar denied the allegations.

perspectives.body: DR reports that 14 countries formally recognised the ruling, including the UK. Denmark has not issued a formal recognition following the judgment, although it joined the case at the court in 2023.

segments.title: A continuing crisis
segments.body: The ruling concerns the 2017 military campaign in Rakhine state, during which about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered, according to the court, and more than 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh. The UK says it will raise the issue at the UN Security Council and is preparing legislation to stop aviation-fuel supplies to Myanmar.

content.headline: Burnham says UK rejoining EU without referendum would be unthinkable
content.shortHeadline: Burnham says rejoining EU would require a referendum
content.standfirst: The prime minister told MPs there is no fixed destination for talks on closer EU ties, but said any return to membership without a referendum would be unthinkable. His comments drew criticism from opponents and former prime ministers.

image.caption: Andy Burnham told MPs he would take a pragmatic approach to the UK’s relationship with the EU.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham says it would be ‘unthinkable’ to rejoin EU without referendum
My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham

segments.body: Andy Burnham said in the Commons that it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without a referendum. He also said his government would take a pragmatic approach to future relations and had no fixed destination, with a plan setting out options due next month.

segments.title: Deal and dissent
segments.body: The agreements reached at last week’s summit cover food and drink checks, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. Burnham says closer ties could help growth and living costs. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him of overselling the deal and turning Britain into a rule-taker; several former prime ministers have warned against reopening the Brexit debate.

segments.title: More talks ahead
segments.body: The UK and EU are set to explore options for closer ties, with discussions on areas including the electricity market and the bloc’s “Made in Europe” scheme. Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election and says the public would decide on any return to EU membership.

content.headline: Government says Freeview switch-off will go ahead; timing still open
content.shortHeadline: Government says Freeview switch-off will go ahead
content.standfirst: The minister responsible says the government has decided to move from terrestrial TV to online-only viewing, with 2034 and 2044 under consideration. Critics warn that internet dependence could leave some households without a reliable service in an emergency.

image.caption: The government says it plans to move to online-only television, despite concerns about emergency access.

sources.originalTitle: The one sentence that kills off the fightback against online-only TV

segments.body: Media minister Ian Murray told MPs the government had decided to switch off digital terrestrial television and move to online-only TV, but had not chosen when. The options being considered are 2034 or 2044. A forthcoming White Paper is expected to recommend a date.

segments.title: Resilience concerns
segments.body: The Lords National Resilience Committee has warned that internet-based television could weaken access to communications during an emergency, particularly if power or broadband fails. The report says about 220,000 UK homes may still lack broadband in the mid-2030s. A campaign group says terrestrial TV remains a backup for more than 10 million households.

segments.title: Different views on the transition
segments.body: Supporters of an earlier switch-off argue audiences are increasingly moving online and say radio and mobile networks should be the focus of resilience planning. The government says the timing will depend on safeguards, infrastructure and access; the dispute over whether to keep a terrestrial backup remains unresolved.

content.headline: Rise of corporate landlords could divide the UK rental market
content.shortHeadline: Corporate landlords grow as renters face a two-tier market
content.standfirst: Build-to-rent homes have tripled since 2019, but remain a small share of the UK market. Supporters point to professional management and amenities; critics warn that smaller landlords are leaving and affordable homes remain scarce.

sources.originalTitle: Britain's landlords are getting bigger. A two-tier rental market may follow

segments.body: Large institutional landlords are expanding in the UK as investment in build-to-rent developments grows. The sector still accounts for about 3% of the rental market, according to Savills, but the number of build-to-rent homes tripled between 2019 and 2025. Most English landlords still own four properties or fewer.

segments.title: Scale brings services—and higher rents
segments.body: Developers say larger operators can invest in maintenance systems, staff and shared facilities. The BBC’s examples show some build-to-rent homes cost more than nearby alternatives, with the higher price partly reflecting amenities such as gyms, concierge services and communal rooms. Tenants’ experiences and priorities differ.

segments.title: Who gets left behind?
segments.body: Tax and regulatory changes have made the market less attractive to some smaller landlords, while rising building costs and interest rates could also slow new developments. Savills’ head of residential research warns that the result could be a two-tier market, with more choice for wealthier city renters and fewer options for lower-income households.

content.headline: Andrew’s £750,000 payment disputed in High Court case
content.shortHeadline: Court hears rival accounts of £750,000 payment to Andrew
content.standfirst: A Turkish businesswoman says she was misled about a payment to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. Her former adviser disputes her account; Andrew repaid the money and is not accused of wrongdoing.

image.caption: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the £750,000 and is expected to give evidence in December.

sources.originalTitle: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told

segments.body: The High Court heard that Nebahat Isbilen says she was misled over a £750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. Her former business adviser, Selman Turk, rejects her allegations and says she knew the payment was intended to seek help for her husband.

segments.title: Disputed payments
segments.body: Isbilen’s lawyers allege Turk misappropriated £38m of her assets and lied about the purpose of the payment to Andrew. Turk’s lawyers argue she understood and directed her own affairs. The court also heard claims about payments to Sarah Ferguson and Princess Beatrice. Andrew repaid the £750,000 and is not accused of wrongdoing.

segments.title: Evidence expected next month
segments.body: Andrew is expected to give evidence in December. The trial is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment to follow. The allegations about the handling and purpose of the payments have not been determined by the court.

content.headline: Met seizes 893kg of suspected cocaine in operation; eight arrested
content.shortHeadline: Nearly 900kg of suspected cocaine seized in London operation
content.standfirst: The Metropolitan Police say they found suspected cocaine hidden in orange boxes at New Spitalfields Market and seized more in a lorry near Maidstone. Eight men have been arrested and remain in custody.

image.caption: Police search boxes of oranges in which suspected cocaine was concealed.

sources.originalTitle: Metropolitan police seize 893kg of cocaine hidden in boxes of oranges

segments.body: Police seized 893kg of suspected cocaine in an operation targeting an alleged organised crime group. Five men were arrested at London’s New Spitalfields Market, where officers found packages concealed beneath boxes of oranges. All eight men arrested in the operation remain in custody.

segments.title: Searches across three locations
segments.body: Police say a sixth man was arrested nearby with a further 100kg of suspected drugs. Officers also seized an estimated £450,000 in cash at a property in Hertfordshire and around 250kg of suspected cocaine from a lorry near Maidstone. The investigation is continuing.

content.headline: UK trial aims to track rogue drones from up to five kilometres away
content.shortHeadline: UK trial to track rogue drones from up to five kilometres away
content.standfirst: A network of antennas will let police identify drones’ remote IDs over a wider area. The government says the trial could inform measures to protect airports and critical infrastructure if the technology proves effective.

image.caption: A proposed antenna network is intended to help police identify drones over a wider area.

sources.originalTitle: UK to deploy new ‘sky shield’ drone trackers to thwart Putin threats

segments.body: A trial will test a network of antennas designed to help police identify drones from as far as five kilometres away. Currently, officers may need to be close to a drone to read its remote identification details. The first use is expected to include incidents at football matches and outdoor concerts.

segments.title: Possible use near airports
segments.body: Aviation Minister Keir Mather said lessons from a successful trial could be applied around airports and critical infrastructure. The Civil Aviation Authority has warned that organised drone activity could disrupt British airports. The trial’s effectiveness and the extent of any future rollout are not yet known.

segments.title: Enforcement and legitimate uses
segments.body: The government says police could use identification data to find drone operators and enforce flight restrictions. Mather also said better management of airspace could support commercial uses, including medical deliveries. The trial is intended to test detection and tracking, not to establish that every drone can be identified.

content.headline: Dyslexic workers report stress and concealment, survey finds
content.shortHeadline: Survey: 46% of dyslexic workers hide it at work
content.standfirst: A British Dyslexia Association survey of more than 1,200 working adults found that 46% conceal their dyslexia and 81% say it adds to work-related stress. The association is calling for more accessible workplaces and trained managers.

image.caption: Ayana Bailey says she relies on her mother to help with job applications.

sources.originalTitle: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic

segments.body: Nearly half of working dyslexic adults surveyed by the British Dyslexia Association said they hide their dyslexia at work, and 81% said it adds to their work-related stress. The survey included more than 1,200 people. The association estimates that 3.3 million dyslexic adults are in employment in the UK.

segments.title: Barriers at work
segments.body: Ayana Bailey, 19, says she does not always disclose dyslexia when applying for jobs because she worries it could count against her. Nurse Lisa Daniels says she struggled with paperwork and that an earlier manager dismissed her request for adjustments. She later found support through a workplace neurodiversity network.

segments.title: Calls for adjustments
segments.body: The association wants employers to make reasonable adjustments even when staff do not have a diagnosis, and for managers to receive training. Lawyers and dyslexia advocates cited by the BBC say inaccessible applications and workplace processes can discourage people from seeking support and obscure their strengths.

content.headline: Experts warn children can encounter extreme violence through social media
content.shortHeadline: Experts warn social media exposes children to extreme violence
content.standfirst: A Danish 11-year-old was allegedly drawn into an online network and coerced into self-harm, TV 2 reports. Child-protection groups warn that violent material also reaches young users through mainstream platforms and feeds.

sources.originalTitle: Børn møder ekstrem vold på sociale medier, advarer organisationer

segments.body: TV 2 reports that an 11-year-old Danish girl was drawn into an online network associated with nihilistic violent extremism and allegedly coerced into harming herself. Two Danish teenagers have been charged in connection with threats and the sharing of recordings, the report says.

segments.title: Violent content can find its audience
segments.body: Experts from Save the Children and Børns Vilkår say children may encounter violent videos through mainstream social media without seeking them out. Some material is disguised with childlike images, a format described as “cutegore”. The Danish Centre for Documentation and Counter Extremism says it has received more concern reports than ever before over the past year.

segments.title: Calls for platform action
segments.body: Save the Children says the share of children reporting a digital violation or unpleasant online experience in the past year rose from 42% in 2021 to 66% in 2026. Experts warn that repeated exposure can normalise violence and say platforms are not doing enough to protect children.

content.headline: Denmark’s 2027 tax forecast opens with new deductions to check
content.shortHeadline: Tax forecast opens: check income, deductions and new relief
content.standfirst: The 2027 preliminary tax assessment is open, and experts urge people to check their income, interest and commuting deductions. New relief includes deductions for some fitness and music activities and a larger employment deduction for older workers.

image.caption: The preliminary tax assessment estimates how much tax people should pay next year.

source.credit: Foto: Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Forskudsopgørelsen er åben – kan man med fordel sætte indkomsten højere eller lavere?
Din forskudsopgørelse er klar: 'Seniorer i beskæftigelse står øverst på vinderskamlen'

segments.body: The Danish Tax Agency has opened the preliminary tax assessment, which estimates how much tax people should pay during 2027. TV 2 and DR’s financial experts advise checking that income, loan interest and commuting details reflect expected changes in work, housing or family circumstances.

segments.title: New deductions
segments.body: People over 30 may be able to claim a deduction for qualifying fitness, yoga, dance, singing or music activities. The deduction is capped at 1,800 kroner for 2027, equivalent to a tax saving of about 470 kroner if used in full. An expanded employment deduction for workers within five years of state pension age is also due to apply.

segments.title: Check before accepting a tax loan
segments.body: Commuting deductions depend on actual travel to work, and the temporarily increased deduction for fuel costs in 2026 will not carry over unchanged to 2027. Homeowners should also check whether they are enrolled in a property-tax deferral loan: it postpones payment but creates debt and interest.

content.headline: High Court rejects discrimination claim over Nøjsomhed evictions
content.shortHeadline: High Court rules Nøjsomhed evictions were not discrimination
content.standfirst: The Supreme Court upheld a ruling that evictions linked to a redevelopment plan in Helsingør’s Nøjsomhed housing area did not amount to direct or indirect ethnic discrimination in this case. The tenants’ lawyer said he was disappointed.

image.caption: Nøjsomhed in Helsingør, which was placed on the government’s parallel-society list in 2018.

sources.originalTitle: Højesteret: Opsigelser i ghettoområde var ikke diskrimination

segments.body: The Danish Supreme Court ruled that the termination of leases in seven blocks of Nøjsomhed, in Helsingør, did not constitute direct discrimination on the basis of ethnic origin. It upheld an Eastern High Court judgment from 2022.

segments.title: The redevelopment plan
segments.body: The housing area was placed on the government’s parallel-society list in 2018. In 2020, the housing association notified tenants in seven blocks that they would have to move as part of a major refurbishment. The residents argued that the evictions discriminated on ethnic grounds.

segments.title: What the court decided
segments.body: The court also found there was not enough information in this case to establish indirect discrimination. The ruling concerns the particular evictions and redevelopment plan; it does not determine other residents’ cases, including protests over evictions in Copenhagen’s Mjølnerparken.

content.headline: Five crew rescued from Danish fishing boat after distress call
content.shortHeadline: Five crew rescued from Danish fishing boat after distress call
content.standfirst: A Danish fishing boat sent a distress signal about 47 nautical miles from Thisted. Five crew members were brought safely to Hanstholm; the cause of the emergency remains unknown, though a captain reported seeing smoke and occasional explosions.

sources.originalTitle: Forsvaret sendte redningshelikopter efter nødsignal fra dansk skib

segments.body: Five crew members from a Danish fishing boat were rescued after a distress signal prompted Danish and Norwegian rescue helicopters to respond. The Danish helicopter returned to Aalborg without the crew, who were taken to Hanstholm by a rescue boat.

segments.title: Cause not confirmed
segments.body: The distress call came from about 47 nautical miles off Thisted. The Danish Joint Rescue Coordination Centre said it remained unclear why the signal was sent. A captain on the vessel that transported the crew told TV MIDTVEST he saw heavy smoke and occasional explosions from the boat.

content.headline: Tarkowski's first Premier League red leaves Everton without captain for derby
content.shortHeadline: Tarkowski's first top-flight red rules him out of derby
content.standfirst: James Tarkowski was sent off in Everton's 4-0 defeat at Brentford, ending a run of 351 Premier League appearances without a red. He will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby, while the decision remains disputed.

sources.originalTitle: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?

segments.body: Everton captain James Tarkowski was dismissed after a VAR review in Monday's 4-0 loss at Brentford. It was his first Premier League red card, and it means he will be unavailable for Sunday's Merseyside derby. The defeat was Everton's heaviest since David Moyes returned as manager.

segments.title: A disputed decision
segments.body: The referee initially showed Tarkowski a yellow, then changed it to a red after reviewing the challenge. The Premier League match centre cited the high studs and contact on the shin. Opinions were divided: some pundits called it harsh, while Jamie Carragher and Toby Alderweireld backed the sending-off. Moyes said he was unsure whether there was enough force.

content.headline: Man Utd's slump leaves Pochettino nine games before squad changes
content.shortHeadline: Pochettino faces nine games before Man Utd can strengthen
content.standfirst: After a 4-0 defeat in his first game, Mauricio Pochettino must try to steady Manchester United from within: the club has nine matches before it can change its squad in January.

sources.originalTitle: 'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?

segments.body: Manchester United are second from bottom after losing 4-0 at Liverpool in Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge. Midfielder Kobbie Mainoo described the team as being at its lowest and said the players had to work together. Pochettino's immediate task is to make a defence that has conceded 19 goals in six games harder to break down.

segments.title: No quick fixes
segments.body: United have nine matches before the January transfer window can bring squad changes. A striker is viewed as a priority, with Benjamin Sesko out until at least January, and the club also has a longstanding issue at left-back. The report notes substantial outstanding transfer fees and says no simple solution to the club's predicament is apparent.

content.headline: De Bruyne says his affection for Man City will survive any title stripping
content.shortHeadline: De Bruyne's loyalty endures as Man City appeal financial verdict
content.standfirst: Kevin De Bruyne returns to the Etihad with Napoli on Tuesday and says his feelings for Manchester City will not change, even if the club lose titles after being found guilty of financial-rule breaches.

image.caption: Kevin De Bruyne, who won 16 trophies during his time at Manchester City.

sources.originalTitle: De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change'

segments.body: Kevin De Bruyne says he still has affection for Manchester City, where he won 16 trophies, and that it would remain even if the club were stripped of titles. He returns to the Etihad on Tuesday with Napoli, having left City in 2025.

segments.title: The case remains unresolved
segments.body: An independent commission found that City breached financial rules, including arranging what it called sham contracts. The club denies wrongdoing and is appealing; any sanctions are still to come. De Bruyne said he could not change the allegations or other people's opinions, and that he was proud of his own playing career.

content.headline: UK nations confirmed as hosts of the 2035 Women's World Cup
content.shortHeadline: UK nations confirmed as 2035 Women's World Cup hosts
content.standfirst: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 48-team tournament, the first football World Cup in the UK since 1966. Some hosting details remain unsettled.

sources.originalTitle: UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms

segments.body: Fifa has confirmed England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales as co-hosts of the 2035 Women's World Cup. The 48-team tournament is planned to feature 104 matches over 39 days. The four nations were the only bidders, and their joint bid was ratified at a special Fifa Congress meeting.

segments.title: Details still to be settled
segments.body: The bid proposed 19 venues across the four nations. Fifa has yet to decide whether all the hosts will qualify automatically, and its evaluation noted outstanding discussion around some government guarantees, including tax and safety and security. The UK government also announced a goal of one million more girls playing, watching or taking leadership roles in sport by 2035.

content.headline: Raya to miss Arsenal's Dortmund game, but early tests rule out surgery
content.shortHeadline: Raya out against Dortmund as Arsenal await further tests
content.standfirst: David Raya will miss Arsenal's Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund with a shoulder injury. Mikel Arteta says early tests are encouraging and surgery is not needed, but more checks are due.

image.caption: Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

sources.originalTitle: Raya to miss Dortmund game but injury 'not serious'

segments.body: Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya will miss Tuesday's match against Borussia Dortmund after hurting his left shoulder in Saturday's draw with Newcastle. Manager Mikel Arteta said early tests were encouraging and that Raya does not need surgery, but further tests were due on Tuesday.

Arteta said the initial pain had raised fears of a more serious injury. The manager identified Kepa Arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier as the other goalkeepers Arsenal can call on. The length of Raya's absence was not yet known.

content.headline: Penge wins four-man play-off for first PGA Tour title and 2027 card
content.shortHeadline: Penge wins first PGA Tour title and secures 2027 card
content.standfirst: England's Marco Penge birdied the first extra hole to win the RSM Classic in Georgia, claiming a first PGA Tour title and the $1.3m prize after a four-player tie.

image.caption: Marco Penge, a three-time winner on the DP World Tour.

sources.originalTitle: Penge wins first PGA Tour title to claim 2027 card

segments.body: Marco Penge shot a five-under 65 to reach 16 under and join a four-man play-off at the RSM Classic. He won it with a birdie on the first extra hole, securing his first title on the main professional tour in North America and the $1.3m top prize.

segments.title: A card secured
segments.body: Penge began the week 120th in the FedExCup standings and needed at least a top-four finish to guarantee full playing status on the PGA Tour next season. He said keeping his card was his first task. After a six-week break to deal with a viral illness and vertigo, he described the work of feeling like himself again.

content.headline: De Villiers alleges Australia tampered with the ball from the first 2018 Test
content.shortHeadline: De Villiers alleges ball-tampering began in first 2018 Test
content.standfirst: AB de Villiers says Australia altered the ball in the Durban series opener, extending renewed scrutiny of the 2018 scandal. Cameron Bancroft has said sandpaper was not used in that match.

image.caption: Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers.

sources.originalTitle: De Villiers claims ball-tampering from first 2018 Test

segments.body: Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged that Australia tampered with the ball in the first Test of the 2018 series in Durban, saying he had no doubt it happened. His claim goes beyond the already disputed allegations about the following match in Port Elizabeth.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts
segments.body: Cameron Bancroft wrote last week that sandpaper was not used in Durban and described other ball-maintenance methods. Australia players and then-coach Darren Lehmann have denied knowledge of tampering during the series. Cricket Australia's voluntary forum for people involved is not a full investigation and will not bring new penalties.

content.headline: CAS to rule on Senegal's appeal in Afcon title dispute
content.shortHeadline: CAS to decide Senegal's appeal over Afcon title
content.standfirst: The Court of Arbitration for Sport is due to decide Senegal's appeal after an African football ruling stripped the team of the 2025 Afcon title it won on the pitch and awarded it to Morocco.

sources.originalTitle: Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case

segments.body: The Court of Arbitration for Sport is due to rule on Tuesday on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip it of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title. Senegal beat hosts Morocco 1-0 after extra time in January, but a Caf appeals board later ruled that Senegal had forfeited the final and awarded Morocco a 3-0 win.

segments.title: A final decision
segments.body: Morocco's federation argued that Senegal breached competition rules when players and staff left the pitch during the chaotic final. Senegal's federation called the ruling unfair and unprecedented. Cas is the final arbiter for bodies that recognise its authority; the result of the appeal was not yet available in the gathered reporting.

content.headline: Stella Z turns field recordings and lucid dreams into ambient soundscapes
content.shortHeadline: Stella Z’s ambient dreams draw on recordings from China
content.standfirst: The Fujian-born, London-based producer builds a nocturnal collage from sounds gathered on trips to China. Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming drifts between ambient, dub and acid, with unease sometimes lending its most vivid moments their charge.

image.caption: Stella Z, the Fujian-born, London-based producer.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming

segments.body: Sounds recorded on Stella Z’s trips to China—among them a pharmacy and the Fujian mountains at night—give Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming its unusual sense of place. Across eight tracks, whispers, percussion and electronics create an unsettled, dreamlike collage.

The album moves through ambient and new-age expanses, with traces of 1990s downtempo, acid and dub. “Exit, Elsewhere” grows disorientating through overlapping narration and rattling bells; a remix by Valentina Magaletti turns the original’s wistfulness into something harsher. Even its clumsier passages help conjure a woozy wilderness.

content.headline: Kate Nash turns music-industry frustration into a fight for touring artists
content.shortHeadline: Kate Nash challenges a music business that makes touring precarious
content.standfirst: The singer’s OnlyFans-funded “Butts for Tour Buses” campaign made the cost of touring hard to ignore. Her forthcoming album Cailín draws on Irish roots, while she argues that fair pay for working musicians requires more than goodwill.

image.caption: Kate Nash.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

segments.body: In 2024, Kate Nash used an OnlyFans account to help fund a tour and staged a protest outside Spotify and Live Nation. She says even artists with established catalogues struggle to make touring work, while friends sell instruments or abandon the road altogether. Without small and mid-sized gigs, she argues, the wider music culture is at risk.

segments.title: A record rooted in family history
segments.body: On Cailín, recorded in Spiddal on Ireland’s west coast, Nash combines traditional instruments with punk and hip-hop as she explores her Irish heritage. The album includes a cover of Sinéad O’Connor’s “Famine”, and follows Nash’s discovery that her grandfather was among men imprisoned while trying to travel to Spain to fight Franco.

segments.title: Making a case for change
segments.body: Nash says the music industry will not reform itself and argues that legislation is needed to make payment fairer. Her account traces the distance between early fame and a career she has rebuilt on her own terms, including acting work and an independent approach to making music.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn grief into playful, personal pop
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul get personal on a new album
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s second album, Mainland Madinina, follows a period of grief and becoming parents. Their familiar wit remains, but the new songs also make room for vulnerability, family history and questions about what gets passed on.

image.caption: Bolis Pupul and Charlotte Adigéry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: After the sharp, politically minded pop of their debut, Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul describe their forthcoming album as more introspective. They began writing it after Adigéry’s father died, and worked on early demos during a trip to Martinique, her parents’ birthplace.

segments.title: Humour alongside grief
segments.body: The record still makes room for absurdity: “Googoo Gaga” plays with parenthood, while “From Healer to Dealer” sends up wellness language. But closing song “I’m Lost” turns toward Adigéry’s grief, as she sings about finally throwing away flowers from her father’s funeral. The album also considers how becoming a parent can bring family trauma into focus.

segments.title: Pop as a Trojan horse
segments.body: The duo say they first recognised the political reach of their music when a Manchester crowd sang along to the deliberately provocative chorus of “Blenda”. Their aim, they explain, is to trust listeners to understand the joke and the ideas carried inside the pop.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s debut solo album makes centuries of folk feel immediate
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat brings centuries of folk into the present
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer gathers songs from Irish, British and American traditions, centring complex women’s stories. Her commanding voice anchors arrangements that move from stark folk to a striking trip-hop reworking.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: Radie Peat opens No Human Tongue Can Tell with the traditional “Hares on the Mountain”, her voice coming in before the piano. The Lankum and ØXN singer plays nearly every instrument on this solo debut, building layered choruses around a voice the review describes as an arresting contralto.

segments.title: Songs that speak across time
segments.body: Peat draws on Irish, British and American songbooks, with particular attention to women whose choices are constrained. The tracklist sets older songs alongside more recent compositions, finding connections between a story of abuse and Liam Weldon’s lament for the frustrated promise of Irish independence.

The boldest transformation is “The Moon and Stars”, which turns the archived fiddle tune “Maid Lamenting” into a trip-hop piece with a skittering beat and surging keyboards. Peat’s performance cuts through the dense production, drawing the album’s distant musical eras into a vivid present.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic instrumentation into a volatile debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop collide with Arabic instrumentation
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist Zeynab Marwan puts her voice at the centre of a dramatic mix of hyperpop production and Arabic instruments. The result connects club aggression to longing and belonging.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: As Thoom, Zeynab Marwan joins producers Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman on a debut that brings hyperpop into contact with Arabic instrumentation. Her voice shifts from syrupy melody to a more menacing edge, and the review hears an artist moving beyond the more atmospheric approach of her earlier releases.

segments.title: Fury and feeling
segments.body: Tracks such as “Janani” and “On the Floor” build around forceful drums and mizmar, while “Morocco” uses oud and slower machines to frame a lover’s hurt. The review praises the way the production amplifies Marwan’s performances, though it finds some of the more conventional songs less distinctive.

The closing song, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon”, holds together a farewell to a lover and a desire to return to Marwan’s homeland. Its unanswered questions about return and renewed conflict give the album’s themes of attachment and uncertainty their clearest expression.

content.headline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue shows how a once-overlooked album shaped indie-pop
content.shortHeadline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue points toward indie-pop’s future
content.standfirst: The band’s 2001 move toward warm synth-pop, once overshadowed by its earlier work, sounds newly influential on a 25th-anniversary edition. The review also finds fresh life in a set of archival live performances.

sources.originalTitle: Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Recorded after drummer Bill Berry’s retirement, Reveal shifted R.E.M. toward a more reflective sound, with strings and electronics replacing some of the band’s earlier rock mysticism. The review argues the album’s dreamy, synth-pop arrangements now look like a precursor to later indie-pop.

segments.title: A reissue with room to roam
segments.body: The review singles out “All the Way to Reno (You’re Gonna Be a Star)” and “Imitation of Life”, while bonus material captures the expanded band playing for Radio France. Familiar songs take on different textures in performance, from organ in “So. Central Rain” to piano and massed vocals on “It’s the End of the World as We Know It (and I Feel Fine)”.

content.headline: Kim Deal’s Barbican concert album lets her personality shine through
content.shortHeadline: Kim Deal’s live album adds orchestral warmth to her songs
content.standfirst: A 13-piece orchestra and choir expand the arrangements from Kim Deal’s solo debut on this London concert recording. It is less a radical reinvention than an affectionate showcase for her distinctive voice.

sources.originalTitle: Live at the Barbican

segments.body: Recorded at London’s Barbican, the concert album draws mostly on Kim Deal’s solo debut, with a few earlier solo songs and Breeders material. The orchestral arrangements largely stay faithful to the studio versions, but the review finds that their strings and brass add subtle warmth and scale.

The orchestra makes a particular difference on “Beautiful Moon”, where cello gives the spare original a more haunting shape. The Shards choir is less prominent, but Deal herself takes centre stage: her rough-edged, expressive delivery brings vulnerability and force to “Walking With a Killer”.

content.headline: Threshold’s new folk-prog sound leads a week of adventurous tracks
content.shortHeadline: Threshold leads a week of adventurous new tracks
content.standfirst: Isaac Eiger’s solo project moves beyond the jangle-pop of Strange Ranger toward folk and loose, minimalist prog. The Guardian’s weekly picks also span experimental pop, UK rap, jazz and more.

image.caption: Threshold, Isaac Eiger’s solo project.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold

segments.body: Threshold’s “Stillwater” stretches out like a wintry walk, drawing on 1970s singer-songwriter piano ballads while pointing toward the wider sound of Isaac Eiger’s forthcoming debut album. The former Strange Ranger frontman’s new material reaches into traditional folk and minimalist prog, leaving his earlier jangle-pop behind.

segments.title: More to hear this week
segments.body: The roundup’s other picks include Heavensouls’ ten-minute experimental piece, a noirish collaboration from BexBlu and Paul Stephan, new tracks from Erika de Casier and Rema, and music by Studio20, Kacey Musgraves and Brazilian duo João Bosco and Guto Wirtti.

content.headline: Paul Schrader embraces AI for filmmaking, even as he fears what it may unleash
content.shortHeadline: Paul Schrader is using AI—and worries it could outgrow him
content.standfirst: The Taxi Driver writer is testing AI-generated actors, scripts and hallucinations for new projects. He sees the technology as hard to resist, but says asking it to write in his own style left him frightened by its capabilities.

image.caption: Paul Schrader, who is experimenting with AI in filmmaking.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80

segments.body: At 80, Paul Schrader is using artificial intelligence to develop films, including horror-thriller The Doors of Perception, which will feature AI-generated psychedelic visions. He has also tested synthetic actors and says the technology could make a whole film, while giving him an unusually easy route around the costs and delays of conventional production.

segments.title: A tool that unsettled its user
segments.body: Schrader says an AI system proposed premises for a script in his style, then produced a scene-by-scene outline and a formatted opening scene. The speed and resemblance to his own writing startled him. “I realised it could write a Paul Schrader script. I got scared,” he said.

segments.title: Hollywood’s unresolved argument
segments.body: While unions and institutions have tried to set limits on AI in film, Schrader believes financial incentives will make it difficult to stop. He also voices a much broader fear that humans may have no lasting place in a world shaped by increasingly capable machines; what remains unclear is how audiences will respond to films made this way.

content.headline: Wicker’s knowingly sexist fairy tale turns a perfect husband into a provocation
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s impossible husband makes for a provocative comedy
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of twigs in this bawdy medieval fantasy. Its reviewer enjoys the comedy but questions the story’s vision of a partner whose own desires barely count.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a lonely fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker to create her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s woven creation is attentive, attractive and seemingly devoted to pleasing her, setting off lust, envy and alarm in the village around them.

segments.title: Fantasy with a sharp edge
segments.body: The review relishes the film’s bawdy humour and argues that its fantasy of a considerate partner responds to familiar inequalities in heterosexual relationships. But it also sees a troubling premise: the husband’s agency is barely explored, and his wife’s wishes take priority even when he objects.

The reviewer finds the film’s contradictions hard to dismiss—and ultimately enjoys it. Colman’s fisherwoman seems to want kindness rather than obedience, but the story’s deliberately excessive reversal raises a question it does not quite resolve: when devotion is built into a partner, can it be freely given?

content.headline: Josephine asks what happens after a child witnesses sexual violence
content.shortHeadline: Josephine explores a child’s trauma after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Director Beth de Araújo draws on her own experience for a drama about an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape. The film’s approach has prompted debate over how cinema should depict sexual violence and protect young performers.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes

segments.body: In Josephine, an eight-year-old girl witnesses a rape in a park, an event that shapes the story of her and her parents, played by Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan. Writer-director Beth de Araújo says the film draws on her own childhood experience and asks how a young person might understand violence before having words for it.

segments.title: Questions about showing violence
segments.body: The film depicts the assault from a distance through the child’s perspective. Film scholar Tanya Horeck says there is no single feminist rule for representing rape on screen, but asks what a scene is doing and whose perspective it serves. She finds the case for placing the scene early in Josephine compelling because the film follows the child’s trauma.

segments.title: Protecting a young actor
segments.body: Reeves, who was eight during filming, did not read the script or appear during the assault scene, and has not seen the finished film. De Araújo says a child psychologist was available to the family and that Reeves can choose whether to watch the film when she is 18.

content.headline: Oobah Butler’s pranks expose how easily industries can be gamed
content.shortHeadline: Oobah Butler turns industry loopholes into comedy
content.standfirst: In a new series, the prankster infiltrates sectors from wellness to music, testing their appetite for bogus products and manufactured hype. The review finds the stunts funny—and an unsettling look at gullibility and weak regulation.

image.caption: Oobah Butler in Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

sources.originalTitle: Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow review – these audacious pranks are tell-your-friends funny

segments.body: Oobah Butler’s five-part series takes his stunts inside industries including wellness, wine, dating, music and royalty. He sells fake wellness products, markets smoke-damaged wine at a premium and tries to make a machine-written song trend, presenting the schemes as experiments as well as jokes.

segments.title: The joke has a target
segments.body: The review praises Butler’s boldness and argues that his pranks mostly take aim at institutions rather than individuals. A former Theranos executive even appears to advise him on marketing, a pointed detail in a show about how readily dubious claims can be sold.

Behind the comic set-ups, the series finds loopholes, weak regulation and investors willing to back far-fetched schemes. The review’s broader verdict is that Butler’s pranks are both disquieting and unexpectedly reassuring: they expose how easily systems can be exploited, while making their targets laughable.

content.headline: The BBC is putting some Christmas specials on iPlayer weeks early
content.shortHeadline: The BBC is moving some Christmas TV specials earlier
content.standfirst: Several festive programmes will arrive on iPlayer from 27 November, ahead of their television broadcasts. The BBC says a longer streaming window reflects viewing habits, while the change leaves questions about the shared ritual of Christmas TV.

image.caption: Mary Berry filming her Christmas Countdown.

sources.originalTitle: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?

segments.body: The BBC plans to make several Christmas specials available on iPlayer from 27 November, in some cases almost a month before they air on television. The broadcaster says viewing of festive programmes has grown earlier in the season and that the longer window may help programmes find an audience.

segments.title: A change to a shared schedule
segments.body: Some major Christmas broadcasts, including the Strictly special and the new Call the Midwife prequel, remain scheduled for television as usual. Radio Times editor Shem Law says the earlier streaming releases may nevertheless weaken the appeal of gathering around a programme together when it finally airs.

content.headline: Melania’s two-part TV documentary offers little beyond its subject’s image
content.shortHeadline: Melania’s TV documentary is more advert than series
content.standfirst: A review finds the two short episodes almost empty of substance, apart from a brief encounter with people affected by natural disasters. The programme repeatedly turns its attention back to Melania Trump and her projects.

image.caption: Melania Trump.

sources.originalTitle: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

segments.body: The review describes Melania as two episodes of short, disconnected scenes rather than a substantial series. It criticises the programme’s polished footage and vague statements, including an extended sequence in which Melania Trump considers the placement of a brooch.

A visit with people affected by Hurricane Helene and wildfires briefly shifts the programme toward their experiences. But the review says it soon returns to Trump’s own initiatives, leaving little room for the people the series appears to be documenting.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the consequences of toxic masculinity in the foreground
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows the cost of toxic masculinity for women
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s coercive behaviour escalates in the latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s drama anthology. The review argues that the series centres the women who are often overlooked in stories about male violence.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: Helen, played by Nicola Coughlan, is in a seemingly ordinary relationship until her partner Steve chokes her without consent during sex. The review focuses on the aftermath: he presents himself as the victim, and Helen ends up apologising before their life returns to normal.

segments.title: The violence of the everyday
segments.body: The review argues that the drama’s disturbing force comes from how ordinary Steve’s behaviour can seem. His grievances about masculinity are reinforced by a friend and grow into coercion and anger, while Helen recognises the pattern but struggles to make him listen.

Rather than centre the destructive man, the episode makes the consequences for his partner its focus. The review sees this shift as an important contribution to television’s treatment of toxic masculinity, while stressing that men’s insecurity does not erase the harm women experience.

content.headline: Black Doves returns with Keira Knightley’s conflicted spy at its centre
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns to its mix of violence and feeling
content.standfirst: The cast and creator discuss the Netflix thriller’s second season, where Helen faces new risks as her husband nears Downing Street. Its murderous antiheroes, they say, work because the show keeps their humour and humanity in view.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Keira Knightley returns as Helen Webb, a spy whose marriage to a politician is bound up with her work for the Black Doves organisation. In the new season, she searches for her missing handler while facing the consequences of her husband’s rise to No 10.

segments.title: Violence with consequences
segments.body: Knightley says the show’s violence can feel like a video game before a sudden moment brings the human cost into focus. Creator Joe Barton says the series tries to acknowledge how violence is normalised in spy stories, even as it asks viewers to care about characters who have killed many people.

Ambika Mod joins as Laila Joshi, a rogue agent who becomes an uneasy ally to Helen. Knightley describes the women’s relationship as an entertaining mix of antagonism and dependence, while Barton says the new season was difficult to shape after several versions of its opening episode.

content.headline: A week’s streaming picks include a new Blade Runner series and Oobah Butler
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Blade Runner 2099, Oobah Butler and more
content.standfirst: A new Blade Runner miniseries and Oobah Butler’s prank-driven show lead this week’s selection, alongside a Buffalo blizzard documentary, Jennifer Lopez in concert and a BBC Christmas ghost story.

image.caption: Michelle Yeoh as Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Cora in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 to Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Blade Runner 2099 brings Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer to a new story in the franchise, while Oobah Butler’s latest series takes his elaborate hoaxes into different industries. Both are among the Guardian’s picks for new films and programmes to stream this week.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: The selection also includes a partly animated documentary about a community sheltering together during a deadly Buffalo blizzard, Jennifer Lopez’s Las Vegas concert film, and a BBC adaptation of a Charles Dickens ghost story. The listings provide a range of options across streaming services and broadcast television.

content.headline: GTA VI claims a record launch, with Rockstar reporting $3.79bn in first-day US$
content.shortHeadline: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79bn on launch day
content.standfirst: Rockstar says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, a figure that would make the game’s launch exceptionally large across entertainment. The company’s estimate has not been independently verified in the supplied reporting.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says

segments.body: Rockstar Games says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, based on the company’s estimates through the end of launch day. The publisher calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history; that comparison is Rockstar’s claim.

segments.title: A record-setting release
segments.body: Rockstar says 32.5 million copies had been sold before release, and that the launch figure is nearly five times the first-day sales reported for GTA V in 2013. The game went on sale for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

The same report notes that police departments urged the public not to imitate the game’s car thefts and other crimes in real life. It also says there is insufficient evidence of a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psychological Association.

content.headline: Elden Ring’s film adaptation faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can an Elden Ring film make its vast world matter?
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has a reported budget near $200m and a major cast, but the game’s horror-tinged fantasy world is not a story by itself. The feature weighs the challenge of giving its setting a reason to hold an audience.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: The Guardian’s feature treats Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation as an unusually high-stakes attempt to bring a vast game world to cinema. The film is reported to be in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman; its budget is said to be close to $200m.

segments.title: A world is not a story
segments.body: The article points to earlier fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate settings into compelling films. Elden Ring’s landscape is especially grim, populated by grotesque creatures and survivors living amid death, leaving open questions about who audiences will follow and what the film’s narrative will be.

Leaked images have prompted speculation that the film may draw on events before the game, but the feature presents that as a possibility rather than a confirmed approach. Garland’s history of resisting conventional reassurance may suit the material, though the scale of the reported budget raises questions about how much freedom he will have.

content.headline: GTA VI is not for children, despite its appeal as a blockbuster game
content.shortHeadline: Why GTA VI’s 18 rating matters for parents
content.standfirst: The review praises Rockstar’s ambitious game but details its explicit sex, drugs and violence. Its central advice to parents is straightforward: the 18 rating signals adult content, not a difficulty level.

sources.originalTitle: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.body: The Guardian’s reviewer calls Grand Theft Auto VI an impressive and sometimes touching game, but says it is among the most explicit they have played. Its crime story includes graphic violence, full-frontal nudity, sex scenes and extensive drug use.

segments.title: A rating is a content warning
segments.body: The piece describes sexual material in the main story and in optional settings, alongside adult dialogue on the game’s fictional radio and television. The reviewer’s concern is not that adults should avoid such content, but that parents may mistake an 18 rating for a measure of difficulty rather than a warning about subject matter.

After more than 70 hours with the game, the reviewer’s advice is that it is not suitable for young children. The article suggests parents consider whether they would let their child watch Breaking Bad, while recognising that older teenagers’ experiences and maturity differ.

content.headline: Keepsake County turns suburban burglary into a melancholy stealth game
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County makes a lonely life of theft playable
content.standfirst: This small stealth game sends a debt-ridden burglar through garish Midwestern homes, where even the loot can be a half-eaten pizza or cheap ornament. Its comic oddities sit alongside a bleak account of financial precarity.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: In Keepsake County, Samuel breaks into suburban homes and steals what he can carry, from golf clubs to half-eaten food. He avoids killing residents, instead tying them up with improvised restraints, and takes his haul to a pawn shop rather than building a conventional arsenal of upgrades.

segments.title: Comedy with a hard edge
segments.body: The review likens the game’s eccentric art and bleak humour to a low-budget television comedy, while noting how Samuel’s medical debts and legal fees make each break-in feel less like a route to success than an act of survival. Its quiet loading-screen landscapes reinforce the character’s isolation.

The game’s repetitive robberies can feel one-note, and the review notes repeated dialogue and limited differences between regions. Yet it argues that the repetition also gives the routine its melancholy force: Samuel has little chance of escaping the conditions that keep sending him back into other people’s homes.

content.headline: Union says it has lost confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.shortHeadline: Union loses confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.standfirst: Prospect says UKRI’s cost-saving plans could damage national science capability and were launched without proper consultation. UKRI’s board and the science minister say they back its chief executive and reform programme.

image.caption: Jodrell Bank Observatory, whose future is at risk under planned UKRI funding changes.

sources.originalTitle: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts

segments.body: Prospect, a union representing scientists and engineers, says it has lost confidence in Ian Chapman, chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), over planned cuts and changes to research facilities. General secretary Mike Clancy urged UKRI to pause its voluntary exit scheme and consult unions on the potential impact.

segments.title: What is at stake
segments.body:
The Science and Technology Facilities Council, part of UKRI, needs to save £162m by 2030. Plans put the future of the UK’s largest telescope at Jodrell Bank at risk, while the Clara accelerator facility is to be mothballed. Other facilities, including Diamond Light Source, are expected to make efficiency savings.

UKRI says it has engaged with staff and research communities and must keep costs within its budget. Its chair, Leszek Borysiewicz, and science minister Chris McDonald both expressed confidence in Chapman and defended the programme as a way to focus resources and deliver value for money.

content.headline: UK hospitals prepare to use Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials conclude
content.shortHeadline: Alzheimer’s blood tests set to reach more UK hospitals
content.standfirst: Some hospitals are introducing a test that may help identify Alzheimer’s within days of a memory-clinic visit, rather than after months or years. Trials are still under way, and access may vary by location.

image.caption: A blood test could help doctors assess people with memory problems for Alzheimer’s.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: A number of UK hospitals are preparing to offer blood tests for Alzheimer’s as part of routine care, with Manchester Brain Health Centre expecting to start within weeks. The test measures a form of tau protein, ptau217, and may help clinicians distinguish Alzheimer’s from other causes of memory problems. University College Hospital in London is already offering it.

segments.title: Earlier diagnosis, uneven access
segments.body:
A faster result could help people and their families plan and may allow some patients to access treatment or clinical trials sooner. Two large trials assessing how the tests fit into NHS services are not due to finish until 2029; hospitals can introduce them earlier, but there is no central register of providers.

That leaves a potential postcode lottery. Doctors also caution that tests bought privately outside a memory-clinic assessment could produce false positives. A blood result is part of a clinical assessment, not a standalone diagnosis.

content.headline: Climate scientists clash over a proposed delay to the IPCC’s next report
content.shortHeadline: Dispute over timing and representation delays IPCC report
content.standfirst: Some governments want the IPCC’s next assessment delayed until after a key climate stocktake, while other countries and scientists warn that a hold-up could weaken global cooperation. The dispute also centres on representation and whose assumptions shape the analysis.

sources.originalTitle: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

segments.body: The IPCC’s next assessment is under way and is hoped to be completed in 2028, in time to inform the 2028 global stocktake under the Paris agreement. Russia, India and the Arab group, including Saudi Arabia, have argued for publication in 2029 instead, saying developing countries are disadvantaged in the process and that some of its assumptions favour richer nations.

segments.title: A dispute about evidence and equity
segments.body:
Potsdam Institute director Johan Rockström says the assessment is an objective synthesis of peer-reviewed research and should not be delayed. Other developing countries, including small island states and least-developed countries, have also called for the work to proceed. The IPCC says 51% of the 664 appointed authors for its three reports come from developing countries and economies in transition.

Lidy Nacpil of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development argues that some emissions-cutting scenarios are biased against the global south, including by assuming that reductions should be made where they are cheapest. The disagreement remains unresolved as the IPCC faces a decision on its budget; without one, completing the reports before the stocktake could be difficult.

content.headline: A string of US outages exposes fragile systems and fuels cyber fears
content.shortHeadline: US outages expose fragile systems and fuel cyber fears
content.standfirst: Recent disruptions to aviation, software, banking and government networks have prompted fears of a coordinated attack, but reporting points to separate technical failures. Experts say ageing infrastructure and a faster pace of vulnerability discovery leave systems under strain.

sources.originalTitle: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

segments.body: A faulty router replacement caused a nationwide US aviation communications failure that cancelled more than 18,000 flights. Other recent disruptions had different causes: a software bug affected Microsoft services, an Apple update caused app outages, and routine maintenance disrupted an internal NSA network. The reporting does not establish that the incidents were connected.

segments.title: Old infrastructure, new pressures
segments.body:
Experts point to ageing systems and the difficulty of replacing them, alongside pressure to patch software flaws found at increasing speed. Some vulnerabilities have been uncovered with AI tools, but the article notes that not all of the bugs are useful to attackers, and that the outages described had separate explanations.

The clustering of incidents has helped conspiracy claims spread online. A cognitive psychologist quoted in the report says transparent, accurate public communication can help counter those explanations. The larger concern is resilience: a single failure should not be able to bring a nationwide system to a halt.

content.headline: Reported hacks hit FBI crime database and US agriculture payment system
content.shortHeadline: FBI and agriculture systems reportedly hacked
content.standfirst: Reports say intruders accessed the FBI’s law-enforcement information network and a US agriculture department payment system. The extent of either breach remains unclear, and officials have not established a link to recent service outages.

sources.originalTitle: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked

segments.body: The FBI’s National Crime Information Center, used by federal, state and local law enforcement to share information including warrants and missing-person records, was reportedly hacked. The US Department of Agriculture’s payment platform was also reported compromised. The scope of the intrusions is not yet clear.

Former officials cited in reporting on the agriculture breach warned that access to the payment database might provide a route to more sensitive information, including food-safety data and research on animal-borne illness. The reports come amid other US service disruptions, but the supplied reporting does not show that these breaches caused those outages.

content.headline: Congress party protesters enter Meta offices in India over suspended accounts
content.shortHeadline: India protest targets Meta over suspended accounts
content.standfirst: Members of India’s opposition Congress party protested at Meta’s Delhi offices, demanding the restoration of party leaders’ Instagram accounts. Two accounts were restored, but the party says many others remain restricted.

sources.originalTitle: Protesters storm Meta offices in India

segments.body: Members of the Congress party’s youth wing protested outside Meta’s Delhi offices on Friday and appeared to enter the building in video shared by CNN. They want the company to restore accounts belonging to party leaders and have warned of further protests. Two of the accounts in question were restored that day.

The party accuses Meta of censoring speech opposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party. Manu Jain, who oversees social media for the Congress youth wing, said thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and government critics remain restricted. Meta had not responded to the report’s request for comment.
