content.headline: An off-Broadway play uses Bluetooth broadcasts to tell a story about hearing
content.shortHeadline: Bluetooth audio turns a play into an experience of hearing loss
content.standfirst: In Love Me, audience headphones carry a character’s clear inner voice while theatre speakers reproduce muffled sound. The Auracast broadcast also supports hearing aids and cochlear implants, making the technology part of both the access and the storytelling.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’

segments.body: The off-Broadway production Love Me gives audience members headphones linked to an Auracast Bluetooth broadcast. The sound design shifts between the speakers in the theatre and audio in the headphones, including a clear inner monologue against muffled external sound, to help convey the central character’s experience of hearing loss.

The production also offers a broadcast intended for compatible hearing aids and cochlear implants, and provides captioned iPads. Auracast enables one audio stream to reach many nearby devices; here, it serves both as an accessibility tool and as part of the show’s form. The reporting describes the technology’s role in this production, not a general assessment of how it performs in other settings.

content.headline: Digital traces can comfort the bereaved, but AI recreations raise questions
content.shortHeadline: Digital memories bring comfort and new questions about grief
content.standfirst: Messages, photos and online memorials can help people stay connected to someone they have lost, while unexpected reminders or AI-generated versions may make grief harder for some. There is no single right way to manage a digital legacy.

image.caption: Kate Woodthorpe, who says digital legacies are likely to grow as more of life moves online.

sources.originalTitle: Are digital memories helping us or holding us back?

segments.body: Digital remnants of someone’s life can offer comfort or feel painful, depending on the person and how their grief changes. Bereavement specialist Karen Sutton advises people to notice whether reminders such as saved messages and phone notifications still help, and to change settings or remove them if they become distressing.

segments.title: What remains online
segments.body:
Sutton worries that AI-generated versions of people who have died could complicate bereavement by creating the impression that the person remains present. Researcher Kate Woodthorpe says the volume of digital material people leave behind is likely to grow as more of life takes place online.

Online spaces can also connect bereaved people: those interviewed describe finding community and support through social media and grief networks. Facebook and Instagram offer memorialised accounts, while some platforms allow families to request account removal.

content.headline: Two organisations say they verified an AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypoth
content.shortHeadline: Two groups verify Alpöge’s AI-assisted Riemann proof
content.standfirst: The Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative say they have independently checked Levent Alpöge’s formalised proof, developed with Claude. That is a major step in assessing the claim, though it is distinct from a prize decision or broad mathematical acceptance.

image.caption: Levent Alpöge, whose Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis was reported as verified by two organisations.

sources.originalTitle: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too

segments.body: Two organisations working with the Lean proof language say they have verified Levent Alpöge’s proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Anthropic mathematician said Claude helped him develop the solution over about six weeks. The Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative said they had full confidence that the proof is correct.

segments.title: What verification does—and does not—settle
segments.body: The result is a notable change from the initial uncertainty around Alpöge’s claim: the groups say the formalised Lean proof checks out. The supplied reporting does not say the Clay Mathematics Institute has awarded a prize or that the result has received general acceptance across mathematics. Making the argument understandable and assessing its wider significance remain part of the process.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch also reports a separate, human-only draft claiming the General Riemann hypothesis, attributed to Alessandro Masullo after 12 years’ work. That draft has not been formalised in Lean, and its correctness and status remain unestablished.

content.headline: Red Cross warns autonomous weapons may outpace efforts to set binding rules
content.shortHeadline: Red Cross warns autonomous weapons may outrun regulation
content.standfirst: After UN talks failed to establish a strong negotiating mandate, the International Committee of the Red Cross says autonomous weapons are advancing faster than regulation. Rights groups warn that delay leaves risks to civilians and the terms of use to militaries and industry.

image.caption: Delegates at the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meeting in Geneva.

sources.originalTitle: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’

segments.body: The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups warn that the development and battlefield use of autonomous weapons may be outpacing international rules. At a week-long Geneva meeting of more than 120 states, efforts to agree a mandate for work on a legal instrument fell short of the urgent action advocates sought.

segments.title: A stalled process, disputed responsibility
segments.body: The Guardian reports that the need for consensus led the conference to adopt a weaker option: countries are to elaborate an instrument by consensus, which may not carry legal obligations. Its reporting describes Russia as leading objections and says the US and other military powers were also reluctant to commit to binding rules. More than 100 states had backed a new legal instrument.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account highlights the consensus rule and the positions of several military powers, including US reluctance to accept a binding treaty. It also reports that a bloc of seven countries pushed for negotiations to begin within a year.

segments.title: Civilian harm and proposed limits
segments.body: The ICRC has called for prohibitions and restrictions, including a ban on using autonomous weapons against people and requirements that systems behave predictably and be limited to military objectives. The Guardian reports civilian deaths in Ukraine and describes concerns about AI-assisted target selection in Gaza and Iran; the supplied reports do not establish that every strike described was carried out by an autonomous weapon.

content.headline: Actor licenses his face for AI microdramas as creators weigh the risks
content.shortHeadline: Actor licenses his likeness for AI-made microdramas
content.standfirst: Aki Avni agreed to let a startup use his likeness in an AI-generated series, presenting a possible new source of work and income for performers. The company has not disclosed the deal’s terms, and critics worry automation could shrink opportunities for actors.

sources.originalTitle: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

segments.body: Israeli actor Aki Avni licensed his likeness to Shortical for Inevitable, an AI-generated microdrama in which a digital version of him plays a fictionalised version of himself. Avni described the project as both exciting and nerve-racking. Shortical says this is its first use of a real person’s likeness and that it hopes the project will draw attention to face licensing.

segments.title: Consent, pay and work
segments.body:
Shortical advertises that people can submit their social-media profiles for possible licensing deals, but says the offer is in its early stages and has not yet led to other signed contracts. The company did not disclose Avni’s compensation or specific terms. Its representative said he was compensated at a level comparable to a non-AI acting role.

Consultant Jennifer Cooper says AI is already unsettling an industry that had offered work to emerging actors. The report also raises the prospect that likeness deals could tie compensation to audience engagement, but does not establish how that model will work in practice.

content.headline: South Korea’s education minister resigns after AI-assisted exam cheating
content.shortHeadline: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal
content.standfirst: A candidate used a concealed camera and smartphone to send exam questions to an AI system, prompting an emergency security overhaul before the national university entrance test. Education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned, citing inadequate preparation.

image.caption: Students at a Seoul high school during South Korea’s university entrance exams.

sources.originalTitle: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

segments.body: South Korea’s education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned after a cheating scandal raised fears that AI could be used to gain an advantage in high-stakes exams. A top scorer in a national tax-accountancy test admitted using a miniature camera to photograph questions, sending them to an AI system and reading answers on a phone.

segments.title: Emergency controls
segments.body: Officials responded with extra supervisors, restrictions on what students could bring, checks for concealed devices and emergency phone alerts. Authorities identified 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices during the university entrance exam, nearly half through the alerts. Choi said he had failed to prepare adequately; the president accepted his resignation.

content.headline: Could AI lending models make credit decisions fairer—or repeat old biases?
content.shortHeadline: AI credit scoring promises inclusion but raises bias concerns
content.standfirst: Lenders are exploring machine-learning tools to assess applicants beyond conventional credit histories, which can leave some people overlooked. Experts warn that opaque models could also reproduce discrimination and make mistaken decisions harder to challenge.

sources.originalTitle: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?

segments.body: Credit scores can shape access to mortgages, loans and phone contracts, but they may not reflect a person’s current ability to repay. The report describes how identity fraud damaged one woman’s score and how a university student was denied a phone contract because she had too little credit history.

segments.title: More data, more accountability
segments.body:
Some lenders and credit firms are testing machine-learning systems that use wider sets of information. Supporters say this could help assess people with limited credit files. But Oxford professor Sandra Wachter warns that systems trained on historical decisions can reproduce social inequalities, while consumer advocates say people need to know what information is used and be able to challenge errors.

The report also describes a credit-reference startup that says it analyses transaction data without AI, citing concern that models could infer sensitive characteristics. The possible benefits of wider assessment remain in tension with privacy, transparency and bias risks.

content.headline: AI tools are making it easier to modify TVs, cameras and other gadgets
content.shortHeadline: AI tools bring device hacking to a wider audience
content.standfirst: Large language models can help users alter gadget software with prompts, extending a long-standing practice beyond experienced developers. The changes may unlock useful features, but can also break devices and leave users outside manufacturer support.

sources.originalTitle: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets

segments.body: A developer used Claude Code to remove unwanted software and redesign the interface on an Android TV. The project drew wide interest and reflects a broader trend: people are using language models to modify camera firmware, music devices and game consoles. The underlying techniques are not all new, but AI tools can make them easier to attempt.

segments.title: New access, new risks
segments.body:
Some manufacturers are embracing custom firmware or open-source tools, while others may respond with tighter controls, digital-rights restrictions or legal action. Modifying a device can also create security and reliability risks; users may have to rely on the same AI tools that made the changes to fix problems.

The developer behind CleanYourTV recommends backing up software and testing in a separate environment. The advice is practical rather than a guarantee: device updates and model changes can still produce problems.

content.headline: South Norfolk MP joins committee shaping data centre policy while opposing local
content.shortHeadline: MP opposing local data centre joins national policy committee
content.standfirst: Ben Goldsborough says data centres are needed but opposes a proposed facility near Norwich, citing local environmental concerns. He has joined a committee that will scrutinise national policy as the government seeks to expand capacity.

image.caption: Ben Goldsborough, the South Norfolk MP who has joined a committee on data centre policy.

sources.originalTitle: MP opposing data centre joins government committee

segments.body: Labour MP Ben Goldsborough, who opposes a proposed 150-megawatt data centre near Norwich, has joined a government committee shaping policy on data centre construction. He says the facilities are needed to support business and new technology, but argues they should be built in the interests of local communities.

segments.title: Growth and local costs
segments.body:
The government wants to expand data centre capacity to six gigawatts by 2030 and is consulting on a draft National Policy Statement. Proposed expectations include investment in local communities, jobs and protection for water supplies. Goldsborough has raised concerns about impacts on nearby nature sites and wants waste heat used to heat homes.

The developer says the Norwich site is well located, near a major road and a substation linked to an offshore wind farm, and could support the local economy. The national policy is still in draft form.
